title: Markov Decision Processes
description: The reinforcement learning problem, returns and discounting, value functions, the Bellman equations, and value and policy iteration.
overview: In supervised learning someone supplies the right answer for every example. In reinforcement learning (RL) nobody does. An agent acts in an environment, sees what happens, and receives a scalar reward that says only how well it is doing, often long after the action that mattered. A chess player learns from a win or loss at the end of the game. A robot learns to walk from falling over. The agent must work out which of its past actions deserve the credit or the blame, and it must try new things to find out whether they are better than what it already does.

The standard mathematical model is the Markov decision process (MDP). This chapter defines it, introduces value functions and the Bellman equations that relate them, and derives the two classical algorithms, value iteration and policy iteration, for computing optimal behavior when the model is known.
objectives: Describe the agent–environment loop and the differences between reinforcement learning and supervised learning.
Define an MDP, a policy, the discounted return, and the Markov property.
Write the Bellman expectation and optimality equations for V and Q.
Run value iteration and policy evaluation by hand on a small MDP.
Explain why value iteration converges and how an optimal policy is read from the optimal values.

sections.title: The reinforcement learning problem
body: At each step t, the **agent** observes a state s_t, chooses an action a_t, and the **environment** responds with a reward r_{t+1} and a new state s_{t+1}. The agent's goal is to choose actions that maximize the total reward collected over time.

list: **Delayed reward and credit assignment**: the reward for an action may arrive many steps later, so the agent must decide which earlier actions were responsible.

**Exploration versus exploitation**: to collect reward the agent should use what it knows (exploit), but to learn what is better it must try the unknown (explore). A restaurant-goer who always orders the same dish may miss a better one.

**The data depend on the agent's behavior**: the examples seen are generated by the policy being learned, so the data distribution shifts as learning proceeds, unlike in supervised learning with a fixed data set.
**Only evaluative feedback**: the reward says how good the action was, not what the best action would have been.

body: Applications include games (Go, Atari, poker), robotics and control, recommendation, resource allocation, and the tuning of language models from human preference feedback.

check.a: Using the best known action to collect reward versus trying other actions to learn whether they are better
wrong: Choosing between a large and a small training set

sections.title: Markov decision processes and returns
body: A **Markov decision process** is a tuple (S, A, P, R, γ):

facts: the transition probabilities: the probability of landing in s′ after action a in state s
the expected immediate reward (it may also depend on s′)

body: The **Markov property** says the next state and reward depend only on the current state and action, not on earlier history: the state summarizes everything relevant. If the agent sees only part of the state (a camera that does not reveal what is behind it) the problem is a partially observable MDP, and the agent must remember or infer.

A **policy** π is the agent's rule for choosing actions. A deterministic policy is a map π(s) = a; a stochastic policy gives a distribution π(a | s). The agent's objective is to maximize the expected **discounted return**, the sum of future rewards, each weighted by a power of γ:

Discounting does several jobs: it keeps the infinite sum finite (at most r_max/(1 − γ)), expresses a preference for sooner reward, and models a chance 1 − γ that the process stops at each step. With γ near 0 the agent is short-sighted; with γ near 1 it is far-sighted.

example.title: Computing returns
example.problem: With γ = 0.9, find the return of (a) a constant reward of 1 forever, and (b) the reward sequence 0, 0, 10 followed by zeros.
example.solution: (a) Σ 0.9^k = 1/(1 − 0.9) = 10. (b) 0 + 0.9(0) + 0.9²(10) = 8.1. The reward of 10 two steps ahead is worth 8.1 now.

sections.title: Value functions and the Bellman equations
body: The **state value function** of a policy π is the expected return when starting in s and following π; the **action-value function** (Q-function) is the expected return after taking action a in s and following π afterward:

eq: Q^π(s, a) = E_π [ G_t | s_t = s, a_t = a ]

body: The return satisfies G_t = r_{t+1} + γG_{t+1}, which gives a recursion, the **Bellman expectation equation**:

eq: V^π(s) = Σ_a π(a | s) [ R(s, a) + γ Σ_{s′} P(s′ | s, a) V^π(s′) ]
Q^π(s, a) = R(s, a) + γ Σ_{s′} P(s′ | s, a) Σ_{a′} π(a′ | s′) Q^π(s′, a′)

body: For a fixed policy this is a linear system, V = r_π + γP_πV, so V^π = (I − γP_π)⁻¹ r_π.

example.title: Evaluating a policy
example.problem: In the two-state MDP of the figure with γ = 0.9, evaluate the policy π: from s₁ move, from s₂ stay.
example.solution: The Bellman equations are V(s₂) = 2 + 0.9V(s₂), so V(s₂) = 2/0.1 = 20, and V(s₁) = 0 + 0.9V(s₂) = 18. The agent earns nothing in s₁, then 2 per step forever.

body: A policy π is at least as good as π′ if V^π(s) ≥ V^{π′}(s) for every s. There is always an **optimal policy** π*, sharing the optimal value function V*(s) = max_π V^π(s) and Q*(s, a) = max_π Q^π(s, a). They satisfy the **Bellman optimality equations**, which replace the average over the policy by a maximum over actions:

eq: V*(s) = max_a [ R(s, a) + γ Σ_{s′} P(s′ | s, a) V*(s′) ]
Q*(s, a) = R(s, a) + γ Σ_{s′} P(s′ | s, a) max_{a′} Q*(s′, a′)

body: Once Q* is known, the optimal policy is greedy: π*(s) = argmax_a Q*(s, a). No look-ahead is needed, which is why Q-functions are the central object of model-free RL.

example.title: Optimal values in the two-state MDP
example.problem: Find V* and π* for the two-state MDP with γ = 0.9.
solution: In s₂, staying forever earns 2 per step: V*(s₂) = 2/(1 − 0.9) = 20.
In s₁: staying gives 1 + 0.9V*(s₁), and moving gives 0 + 0.9V*(s₂) = 18. If the optimum were to stay forever, V = 1/0.1 = 10 < 18, so moving is better: V*(s₁) = 18.

Check: Q*(s₁, stay) = 1 + 0.9(18) = 17.2 and Q*(s₁, move) = 18. The optimal policy moves from s₁ and stays in s₂. A myopic agent that always takes the immediate reward would stay in s₁ for 1 per step (value 10), and be far worse.

check.q: Given Q*(s, a) for all actions, the optimal action in s is
wrong: the action with the largest immediate reward

sections.title: Value iteration and policy iteration
body: If the model (P and R) is known, the optimal policy can be computed with dynamic programming.
Turn the Bellman optimality equation into an update. Start with V₀ = 0 (or anything) and repeat, for all states,

body.eq: V_{k+1}(s) = max_a [ R(s, a) + γ Σ_{s′} P(s′ | s, a) V_k(s′) ]

example.title: Value iteration on the two-state MDP
example.problem: Run three iterations from V₀ = 0 with γ = 0.9.
solution: At first the immediate reward dominates, and the values are short-horizon estimates. By k = 3 the greedy action in s₁ has switched to move. The values climb toward V* = (18, 20).

body: **Why it converges.** The Bellman optimality operator T, defined by (TV)(s) = max_a[R + γΣPV], is a **contraction** in the max norm: ‖TV − TV′‖_∞ ≤ γ ‖V − V′‖_∞. By the Banach fixed-point theorem it has a unique fixed point, V*, and the error shrinks by a factor γ every iteration: ‖V_k − V*‖_∞ ≤ γ^k ‖V₀ − V*‖_∞. With γ = 0.9, reducing the error by a factor of 1000 takes ln 1000/ln(1/0.9) = 66 iterations. When γ is close to 1, convergence is slow.

list: **Policy evaluation**: compute V^π for the current policy, by solving the linear system or by iterating the Bellman expectation equation.
**Policy improvement**: make the policy greedy with respect to V^π: π′(s) = argmax_a [R(s, a) + γ Σ_{s′} P(s′ | s, a) V^π(s′)].

body: The policy improvement theorem guarantees V^{π′} ≥ V^π, with strict improvement somewhere unless π is already optimal. A finite MDP has a finite number of deterministic policies, so policy iteration terminates at π* in a finite number of steps, often very few (a handful of iterations). Each iteration is more expensive than a value iteration step because of the evaluation.

list: Cost: value iteration is O(|S|²|A|) per sweep for tabular MDPs. Policy evaluation by solving the linear system is O(|S|³).

These methods need the model P and R, and a number of states small enough to store a table. Real problems have huge or continuous state spaces (the curse of dimensionality) and unknown models, which is the subject of the next chapter.

For continuous states with linear dynamics and quadratic cost, the optimal control is known in closed form (the **linear quadratic regulator**, LQR), computed by the same backward recursion on value functions.

wrong: always has a zero fixed point
does not depend on the discount factor

check.a: policy evaluation and greedy policy improvement

summary: In RL an agent acts, observes a state and reward, and learns to maximize long-run reward without being told the correct action. The challenges are delayed credit, exploration and data that depend on the policy.
An MDP (S, A, P, R, γ) has the Markov property. The objective is the expected discounted return G_t = Σ γ^k r_{t+k+1}.
V^π and Q^π satisfy the Bellman expectation equations; V* and Q* satisfy the optimality equations with a max over actions. The optimal policy is greedy in Q*.

Value iteration repeatedly applies the Bellman optimality update and converges geometrically at rate γ because it is a contraction. Policy iteration alternates evaluation and improvement and terminates in finitely many steps.
Dynamic programming needs the model and a small state space, which motivates model-free and function approximation methods.

problems.q: In the two-state MDP with γ = 0.5 (all else the same), compute V* and the optimal action in s₁.
problems.solution: V*(s₂) = 2/(1 − 0.5) = 4 (staying). In s₁: staying forever gives 1/0.5 = 2; moving gives 0 + 0.5(4) = 2. The two are equal, so either action is optimal in s₁, and V*(s₁) = 2.
problems.a: V* = (2, 4); both actions are optimal in s₁.

problems.q: A policy in a two-state chain gives rewards (1 per step in state A, 0 in B), and transitions A → A with probability 0.5 and A → B with probability 0.5, B → A with probability 1. With γ = 0.8, evaluate V^π(A) and V^π(B).
How many value-iteration sweeps are guaranteed to reduce the max-norm error by a factor of 10⁶ when γ = 0.95?

An agent in state s has two actions. Q*(s, a₁) = 5.0 and Q*(s, a₂) = 6.5. Write V*(s) and π*(s). If an ε-greedy policy with ε = 0.2 picks the greedy action with probability 1 − ε + ε/2 and the other with ε/2, what is its value in s if it plays optimally thereafter?
problems.solution: V*(s) = 6.5, π*(s) = a₂. The ε-greedy policy chooses a₂ with probability 0.9 and a₁ with 0.1, so its value (using Q* afterwards) is 0.9(6.5) + 0.1(5.0) = 6.35.

problems.q: Why does a discount factor of exactly 1 cause trouble in a continuing task, and how can it still be used?
problems.solution: The return Σ r_{t+k+1} can be infinite, so values are undefined and the Bellman operator is not a contraction. For episodic tasks that terminate with certainty, the sum is finite and γ = 1 is fine. For continuing tasks one can instead maximize the average reward per step.
problems.a: The return may diverge; use γ < 1, episodic tasks, or average reward.
